prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength made possible measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B004 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and after the first round I can state the reason more sharply than before. The subject of the award is a mechanism, not an instrument: at the magic wavelength the differential ac Stark shift of the clock transition vanishes to first order, so a lattice can confine thousands of neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, without disturbing the transition that is being measured. That is a clean, general idea of the kind I trust, and the control of the remaining shifts (blackbody radiation, hyperpolarisability and higher multipole lattice shifts, density shifts and collisions in the Fermi gas) is well-posed theory that has been checked against experiment. It is therefore understood and not merely working. The idea was realised by Katori's group, and Ye's group took it to the 1e-18 frontier and into the many-body regime with a degenerate Fermi gas, with independent reproduction at RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere, so the verification requirement is met. Two names map onto two identifiable decisive contributions. I see no second part that improves the configuration: the alternatives each carry an unresolved problem (attribution for B010 and B034, maturity for B010, overlap and tiny support for B007) that a second seat would import into an otherwise coherent prize.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems is real, and I do not think it can be argued away; it can only be handled by wording. A citation that speaks of precision clocks in general invites the continuation reading, so it must name the magic-wavelength lattice itself. Beyond that, the tests of constancy of constants have so far given null results, so the fundamental-physics argument is currently one of capability and not discovery, and a measurement tool is less of a surprise than a new phase or a new observational window. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened. And two names leave outside the prize Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Hinkley and the SYRTE group, whose early or record demonstrations were important. I also should record that, if the committee preferred a prize about a new state of matter, my own deeper conceptual preference (B007) is blocked by the overlap with the 2016 defect prize and by lack of support, and B010 is not yet mature.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the comb counts optical cycles and does not contain the idea of trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, and that the constants tests and the millimetre redshift measurement show nature being asked a sharp question with a new instrument. He also warns that the count of seven of eight is no substitute for argument.
responses.response: I agree with the first point and it answers the chair's overlap question for me: the comb solved the problem of reading out an optical frequency, whereas the lattice solved the problem of what to put under the comb, namely many neutral atoms with the light shift engineered away. Those are different physical ideas, and the 2012 ion work does not contain either, because a single trapped ion cannot be traded for ensemble statistics without a magic condition. Where I differ is on the foundational framing. The constants tests are so far null results, so I would not rest the citation on them; I rest it on the mechanism and the capability, and treat the redshift and constants work as evidence that the capability is useful beyond metrology. On the count I fully agree, and my own move from B007 to B004 was not made because others had ranked it.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B010 first, on the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments, and says in his case against that a maturity-first reading could put B004 ahead. He also objected in round 1 that the hexatic work (B007) overlaps with the 2016 prize and would have to explain what is new relative to Kosterlitz and Thouless.
responses.response: On B007 you are right and I concede it: Kosterlitz and Thouless supplied the defect-unbinding picture, and the hexatic phase is a continuation that the committee would have to argue is separate, which I cannot do convincingly in this year. On B010 I accept the theory-then-experiment structure as a strength, and I think you are honest to concede the pairing mechanism is open. But your own two reservations carry the weight for me: Cao is outside the credited trio, and an eight-year-old field with an undecided mechanism is where I would wait. If the committee were to ask which of us has to move, I would say the maturity-first reading you describe is the one that decides it, and I would invite you to say plainly whether you now keep B010 first or accept B004, since the chair asked exactly that.

responses.point: Olsson says she cannot settle from memory whether Katori's proposal or the first operational clock marks the original contribution, and that if credit cannot be apportioned to two people without distorting the record, B010 is the better-structured alternative.
responses.response: I think the record supports exactly two names, and I would not move to B010 on this ground. The proposal of lattice trapping at a magic wavelength and its first realisation with strontium are both Katori's, so the origin of the idea and its first demonstration sit with one person, which removes the question of which of the two marks the origin. Ye's contribution is of a different and separable kind: the accuracy and stability records, the degenerate Fermi gas clock and the systematic-uncertainty analysis that made 1e-18 credible. Lemonde, Takamoto and the other groups were important, but I could not point to a decisive contribution that is neither Katori's idea nor Ye's performance step, and none of the other round-1 files has shown one either. B010 has its own attribution problem, since Cao is outside the trio, so it is not the better-structured alternative on this criterion.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, defends B004 as the cleanest combination of original idea, decisive experiment and independent confirmation, and says the citation must be written around the lattice-clock invention itself and not around clocks in general. He also notes that Ye appears in other candidacies.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have worded mine accordingly: 'invention and development of optical lattice clocks' with the magic-wavelength trapping named in the clause. On Ye appearing elsewhere, I do not see why that matters for a single-part configuration; the credit is assessed on the contribution to this achievement, and his contribution here is distinct and large. I would add one qualification to your 'durable' argument: the SI redefinition is expected but has not occurred, so durability rests on reproduction and intercontinental comparison, which are real, and not on adoption by the metrology community, which is still ahead. That is a reason to word the citation around demonstrated performance and not around the redefinition.

responses.point: Kroll values the attribution as unusually tidy, with Katori originating and first demonstrating the concept and Ye driving the systematic-uncertainty records, and sees the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the strongest objection, noting that ion clocks and fountain work are close relatives.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and accept that the overlap is the strongest objection; in round 1 I still saw a continuation risk and I have not fully dismissed it. My view now is that the overlap would be real if the citation were about accuracy, because accuracy is what the ion clocks and fountains also pursued, and would be weak if the citation is about the trapping scheme that makes neutral-atom ensembles usable. The ion clock lineage reaches its limits by having one ion, and the lattice clock exists precisely to escape that limit. That is the distinction I would want written into the citation, and it is the one part of the case I think a sceptical colleague could still contest in the final vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate physical idea from the 2005 comb and the 2012 single-ion control, or reads B004 as a continuation; this depends on the citation wording and is the main risk.

Whether the record is best served by exactly two names, given that Lemonde, Takamoto and the SYRTE group contributed early demonstrations; I find no decisive third contribution but am relying on the first-round files and on memory.
Whether waiting for the SI redefinition of the second would make the award more secure or whether the demonstrated 1e-18 performance is sufficient now.
Whether B010 becomes mature and fairly creditable (Cao, pairing mechanism) in a later cycle, and whether B007 can be separated from the 2016 prize at all.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited candidate: my frequent co-authors and institutional ties (Gothenburg, MPI Stuttgart and Dresden, Oxford, Cornell, Göttingen) do not include Katori or Ye or any shortlisted laureate. I note that I proposed B007 and B027 in the opening and B007 is an alternative here; that is a topical preference, not a conflict. Johansson and Olsson are Chalmers colleagues and my department is neighbouring, which I do not consider a recusal matter. I support Johansson's step-back on B034 and B043, which do not affect my preferred configuration.
